themes.name: MISUNDERSTOOD Subtheme: ALS community feels misunderstood by the FDA
themes.parent: Parent Theme: ALS community feels a significant relational deficit to the FDA
themes.definition: The ALS community (ALSC) lives in a world that is very different from the average human experience. People with ALS live with the knowledge that their days are numbered on the scale of single digits. This plays an immense psychological toll on what they value and how they go about living their lives. From various comments we see incisive prose directed at the FDA for failing to recognize the reality of their lives. Whether or not this truly reflects what the FDA understands about the ALSC, the comments show some perception and grounding that the FDA lacks some of this understanding since these comments are in response to a document representing the FDA’s thoughts around policy. This is most directly interpreted as misunderstanding rather than other possibilities of simple expressions of anger or frustration with reasons of the FDAs inability to make changes if they did understand. The comments look like the comments one would write to get ideas of understanding across even if emotionally charged.

themes.name: PRACTICAL CONSTRAINTS Subtheme: The ALS community has a hard time coming to terms with the idea that FDA systems and practices are subject to practical constraints.
themes.parent: Parent Theme: ALS community feels a significant relational deficit to the FDA
themes.definition: We see various expressions of emotion and backlash toward the FDA from the comments. One would reasonably assume that the FDA is not intentionally doing things to harm the ALSC. In other words, taking the story of the commenters at face value would paint the FDA in a light that contradicts their general role and track record in the world for trying to facilitate safer and improved drug development. One can reasonably assume that there are some real reasons why the FDA has made certain decisions based on its years of experience in their role. This is largely based on the asymmetric incentive structure of the FDA where approving a drug that later causes harm produces visible, attributable blame, while delaying or blocking a drug that would have helped produces invisible costs borne by patients. This asymmetry is also present in research norms and best practices where trial design conventions, statistical thresholds, and endpoint requirements were developed to protect credibility and scientific defensibility, not to optimize for patient timelines. The ALSC does not experience these as structural constraints, but as something that should not be in place, which has real weight given that they are nowhere close to the median environment the FDA has created norms around.

themes.name: ENTITLEMENT Subtheme: The ALS community feels the FDA should have less power over what affects their life.
themes.parent: Parent Theme: ALS community feels a significant relational deficit to the FDA
themes.definition: We see comments expressing that the FDA should not get to control their access to things that so directly affect deep and important aspects of their life. Reading into the implicit emotions, a sentiment is that the FDA is seen as if they are “entitled” and there is strong pushback from the ALS community on this — something reminiscent of discriminated communities fighting for their rights. This is supported by statements that demonstrate direct stated opposition to the power dynamic at play from the FDA to the ALSC, which is the structural parallel entitlement and discrimination.

themes.name: CREDIBILITY Subtheme: Appeal to credibility through personal relation to ALS
themes.parent: Parent Theme: The ALS community utilizes appeals to emotion, logic and credibility in their comments to the FDA
themes.definition: We see comments aimed at the FDA that leverage individual ties to the ALSC in hopes of better leveraging their suggestions for change and furthering understanding of the FDA to the ALSC. We see a variety of relationships to the ALSC shared in the comments. We see people who have ALS directly, who have family relations to those with ALS or who have career relations to those with ALS.

One can infer that the ALS community is eager to right away jump at any opportunity to remedy their situation, and this is seen in the intensity of many comments.

themes.name: LOGIC Subtheme: Appeal to logic through reasoning for suggestions
themes.parent: Parent Theme: The ALS community utilizes appeals to emotion, logic and credibility in their comments to the FDA
themes.definition: We see comments aimed at the FDA that leverage logical reasoning in hopes of changing policy. Reasons used for policy change include new technological advances, other examples of innovation, and personal feelings about usual risks/impediments to innovation that don’t apply to ALS patients.

quotes.text: The recent death of Stephen Hawking relates the fact that ALS akin to certain other neuro-degenerative diseases; care must be taken to ensure that guidance serves to accommodate soon to be coming scientific developments which improve genetic screening which could choose to properly select patients for trials based on genetic variants of the disease and also properly avoid the risk of harm that to patients who may be susceptible to side effects; through modeling methods like ""system on a chip"".

Respect should be given to therapies which are not only curative, but which have the lesser but admirable of being disease modifying for ALS; even if a given therapy is not curative, improvements in swallowing, breathing, digestion or movement all could lead to additional inroads for ALS patients which improve both quantity and quality of life.
This guidance does not reflect the urgency of the disease, nor does it reflect the advances in science and/ or technology that have been made over the last several decades.

Industry must be pushed to embrace update clinical trial design that correlates to the number of people living with ALS, the rapid progression of the disease, the lack of available therapy.  This can be done through the use of historical controls, filling trials by utilizing mobile technology and trial sites, and futility design, among other options.

Widen the inclusion criteria to allow more people with ALS into the clinical trials as they currently are very narrow, not allowing the majority of patients to be able to participate. … We live in a world of great technology, mobile devices have become a part of our everyday lives, use it to benefit clinical trials!

people suffering from this monster of a disease don't have the luxury of time on their side.  … With the FDA taking 12-15 years to approve a drug or treatment option the majority of people suffering from this disease will be gone.

Push for the use of trial designs that realistically represent the number of people living with this disease at one time.

The draft guidance for ALS is completely unacceptable.   … The draft guidance for ALS is completely unacceptable.  This document fails to recognize 1) the severity of this swift, fatal, and indiscriminate disease; 2) that it still lacks treatment; 3) ethical concerns of single-arm trials; and 4) that ALS is non-homogenous and therefore urgently requires newer, innovative trial designs to make possible the discovery of viable therapies.  Furthermore, this input from the patient community was received in guidance document meetings coordinated by ALSA - but removed from the published document.  The patient community has had numerous discussions with Dr. Janet Woodcock in which we received assurances that innovative trial designs are being embraced, and yet - this guidance actually DISCOURAGES THEM.    … This guidance is NOT a representation of the patient community.  … It is neither comparable nor remotely progressive contrasted with other recently released guidance documents for other diseases such as DMD and BCG-Unresponsive Nonmuscle Invasive Bladder Cancer - documents that recognize the ethical concerns and limitations of RCT.
